noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to describe the shapes of s and p orbitals
know that orbitals in sub-shells: i each take a single electron before pairing up ii pair up with two electrons of opposite spin

primer.text: Electron homes have shapes and filling rules. This note draws the spherical s orbitals and perpendicular dumbbell p orbitals, sizes both by shell number, then applies Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle to populate sub-shells singly with parallel spins before any pairing begins.

lessons.title: Drawing s and p shapes
lessons.opening: Orbitals are probability maps, and the map has shapes: s orbitals are spheres, p orbitals are dumbbells on the axes. This lesson sizes and orients both, and fixes what d orbitals are NOT required to look like.
keyPoints: s orbitals are spherical and grow larger with each successive shell.
p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, in sets of three along x, y and z, mutually perpendicular.
Every shell from n = 2 upward carries three p orbitals; the first shell has none.
The d orbital shape is explicitly not required.

low.restatement: Draw s as a circle around the nucleus and p as two lobes pointing along an axis.
low.analogy: An s orbital is a beach ball centred on the nucleus; a p orbital is two balloons tied at the nucleus, pointing one way.
low.examPointer: Say 'dumbbell' and 'perpendicular' - the two keywords examiners scan for.

medium.restatement: The shape encodes where the electron is likely to be found: s probability is angle-independent, while p probability splits into two lobes either side of a nodal plane at the nucleus, one set per axis.
medium.analogy: The s orbital is a fog cloud with no preferred direction; a p orbital is fog split into two lobes with a clear gap at the nucleus.
medium.examPointer: Lobes lengthen as n rises - mention size growth for both s and p when describing shell effects.

check.stem: What shape does an s orbital have?

options.explanation: The s probability cloud is angle-independent: a sphere.
That is the p orbital's shape.
That describes d orbitals - and is not required.

check.stem: How are the three p orbitals of a shell oriented?

options.text: Along the x, y and z axes, perpendicular to one another
options.explanation: Each p orbital claims one axis.

options.text: All three along the x axis
options.explanation: They would be degenerate AND identical, which is impossible.

options.text: Pointing at 45 degrees to each other

options.explanation: The axes are fixed and orthogonal.

options.text: Only the outermost shell of each atom
options.explanation: Every filled shell from 2 up has its own p set.

check.stem: How does the size of s orbitals change with shell number?

options.text: They grow larger as n increases, so 3s is bigger than 1s
options.explanation: Higher shells sit farther out on average.
Both s and p lobes lengthen.

check.stem: What must you know about the shapes of d orbitals?

options.text: Nothing beyond their count and capacity - their shape is not required
options.explanation: The specification stops at s and p shapes.
The d shape is out of scope.

options.text: They only exist in shells 1 and 2

check.stem: Describe the shape and orientation of p orbitals.
check.modelAnswer: Dumbbell-shaped, three per shell from n = 2 upward, pointing along the x, y and z axes at right angles to each other.

check.stem: State the capacities of s and p sub-shells.
check.modelAnswer: An s sub-shell holds one orbital (2 electrons); a p sub-shell holds three orbitals (6 electrons).

check.stem: Explain why the p orbital's shape shows a node at the nucleus.
check.modelAnswer: The p probability distribution splits into two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus with a plane of zero probability through it: the electron in a p orbital is found on either side, never ON the nodal plane at the centre, which is what the dumbbell drawing encodes.

check.stem: Sketch-verbalise the difference between a 2p orbital and a 3p orbital.
check.modelAnswer: Both are dumbbells along one axis, but the 3p lobes are larger and longer, because the third shell's probability cloud extends farther from the nucleus.

lessons.title: Filling rules: Hund and Pauli
lessons.opening: Two rules govern how electrons settle into orbitals: single occupancy first with parallel spins (Hund), then pairing with opposite spins inside full orbitals (Pauli). This lesson shows both in p-sub-shell diagrams and explains the energy logic behind them.
keyPoints: Electrons occupy separate orbitals in a sub-shell singly before any pairing begins.
Paired electrons carry opposite spins, as the Pauli exclusion principle demands.
Spin-pair repulsion drives the single-first strategy.
A 2p electron's energy corresponds to its principal quantum number n = 2.

low.restatement: Fill empty boxes one electron each first, arrows same way; only then double up, arrows opposing.
low.analogy: Bus seating: passengers take empty seats first and sit in the same direction; only a full bus forces sharing - and co-riders face opposite ways.
low.examPointer: Arrows up/down in box diagrams ARE the spin notation - keep them consistent.

medium.restatement: Hund's rule minimises repulsion by maximising single occupancy with parallel spins; Pauli's principle forbids two identical electrons, forcing opposite spins once an orbital must be shared, because the extra pairing energy is still cheaper than climbing to the next empty orbital.
medium.analogy: Room-mate economics: nobody doubles up while single rooms remain; when a room must be shared, the two occupants settle into opposite routines.
medium.examPointer: Three electrons in a p sub-shell: one in each of px, py, pz - the diagram shows three up-arrows, no pairs.

check.stem: Three electrons enter a p sub-shell. Where do they go?

options.text: One each into px, py and pz, all with parallel spins
Two paired in px, one in py
options.explanation: Pairing must wait until every orbital has one.
An orbital holds two electrons at most.

options.text: One in px, two split between py and pz with random spins

check.stem: What does the Pauli exclusion principle state?

options.text: An orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins
options.explanation: The two-rule capacity and spin condition.

options.text: Electrons always spin in the same direction
Each sub-shell fills completely before the next
options.explanation: That is the filling order, not Pauli.

check.stem: Why do electrons single-occupy before pairing, given that they repel each other anyway?

options.text: Because the energy cost of climbing to the next empty orbital is greater than the repulsion of sharing later
options.explanation: Pairing is deferred while cheaper single slots exist.

check.stem: When a fourth electron enters a p sub-shell, what happens?

options.text: It pairs in one of the p orbitals with opposite spin, leaving two singles
options.explanation: The first three took the empty orbitals; the fourth doubles one.
The sub-shell has room for six.

options.text: It enters the s orbital of the same shell
It cannot enter - p is full

check.stem: Electrons with the same spin repel. What is this called and what does it drive?

options.text: Spin-pair repulsion, driving single occupancy before pairing
options.explanation: The repulsion pushes electrons apart into empty orbitals.

check.stem: State Hund's rule in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: Within a sub-shell, electrons occupy separate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any orbital is paired.

check.stem: State the Pauli exclusion principle in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: An atomic orbital can hold at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.

check.stem: Explain why the spin direction is represented by arrows in box notation and why paired arrows must point oppositely.
check.modelAnswer: Electron spin behaves like rotation about its own axis, creating a tiny magnetic moment; box diagrams draw that moment as an arrow, and two electrons sharing one orbital must differ in spin direction, so their arrows run up and down rather than both the same way.

check.stem: Draw-verbalise the box diagram for four electrons in a 2p sub-shell, naming the rule each step obeys.
check.modelAnswer: First three: single arrows up in px, py, pz (Hund's rule). Fourth: pairs into px with a down-arrow, opposite spin (Pauli exclusion principle), leaving py and pz singly occupied.

glossary.definition: A region of space around the nucleus where an electron is likely to be found; each holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
Electrons fill a sub-shell's orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing begins.
No orbital may hold two electrons with the same spin; paired electrons run opposite.
